extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proof-writing / authors of introductory proof-based mathematics homework
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for writing rigorous, readable proofs in an introductory proof-based mathematics course: how to state assumptions, introduce variables, use definitions, structure sentences/paragraphs, and avoid common logical and stylistic errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make specific claims about specific variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements in a proof must refer to specific values (instances of variables) rather than high-level abstract descriptions about all objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arguing at a high level about 'numbers in general.' Introduce particular variables (e.g., “Pick an integer n.”) and manipulate those specific variables. The page gives an incorrect example that reasons abstractly about divisors and concludes without naming variables; such arguments are not rigorous and often cannot be salvaged. When you have an existential fact (e.g., n is even), existentially introduce a variable (there is an integer k where n = 2k) and use it concretely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and properly introduce variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce variables with the correct logical scope: existentially-introduce when you know values exist; do not universally-introduce placeholders when you mean to name specific existing quantities; do not redefine variables incorrectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you assume 'let m and n be integers' you shouldn't later say 'for all integers r and s we have m = 2r' — that incorrectly universalizes r and s. When you are naming witnesses (e.g., m = 2r), treat r as an existentially-introduced variable (there exists r). Don't pick concrete numeric examples when proving a general claim. After an existential introduction you may give a new name to a previously-constructed expression (e.g., define t = r+s) but don't phrase that as a universal choice for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly articulate assumptions and want-to-show
rubrics_metrics.description: At the start of a proof, explicitly state the assumptions (what you've chosen) and what you intend to prove (the want-to-show).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly tell the reader your starting assumptions and your goal (e.g., 'Pick integers m and n. We need to show ...'). This clarifies scope and avoids variable-scoping errors. In proofs by contradiction, restate clearly what the contradictory assumption is and what the intended general conclusion will be once the contradiction is reached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't repeat definitions; use them instead
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not restate definitions in the abstract; apply definitions to the specific variables in your proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sentences that merely restate a definition at a high level (e.g., 'Every even number can be written as 2k'). Instead, apply the definition to your specific variable ('Since n is even, there is an integer k where n = 2k'). Restating definitions can introduce scoping mistakes and makes proofs longer. The page shows three incorrect approaches and the recommended concise phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in complete sentences and paragraphs (mugga mugga test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should be written in grammatically-correct English sentences arranged in paragraphs, not as a sequence of math-only fragments or bullet points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the 'mugga mugga test': replace mathematical content with 'mugga mugga' and check grammaticality. Avoid using mathematical equalities or expressions as the verb of a sentence. Provide explicit subjects and verbs (options given: 'we can write...', 'there is an integer k such that...'). Do not use numbered lists or bullet points as the main structure of proofs. Keep writing concise but complete so the logical flow is readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using mathematical notation as the verb
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't let an equation serve as the grammatical verb of a sentence; restructure sentences so there is an explicit subject and verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show how to change 'Since n is even, n = 2k.' (fails mugga mugga) into 'Since n is even, there is an integer k where n = 2k.' or 'Since n is even, we can write n = 2k.' This preserves mathematical brevity but keeps sentences grammatical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shorthand symbols like ∴ and ∵ and other propositional/connective symbols in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use shorthand logical symbols (quantifiers or propositional connectives) or shorthand notations like ∴ and ∵ in written proofs intended for homework/class writeups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The course forbids ∀, ∃, →, ∧, ∨, ¬ inside written proofs. Use English to express quantification and logical structure. Similarly, avoid shorthand symbols (∴, ∵) that make prose terse and hard to read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid quantifiers and propositional connectives in written proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include formal logical symbols (∀, ∃, →, ∧, ∨, ¬) in the prose of proofs; express logical structure in English sentences instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic and arithmetic symbols (=, +, −, etc.) are fine, but quantifiers and logical connectives should be written out to make proofs clearer and more accessible. The page gives an example transforming a symbolic theorem statement and proof into English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make each sentence load-bearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Every sentence in your proof should contribute to the logical argument; avoid including unused facts or irrelevant statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not state facts that are not used later (e.g., asserting p' ≠ 0 when it is not used). Keep sentences focused and necessary. The page flags issues in examples where extraneous sentences clutter the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not choose specific numeric examples in a general proof
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving a general statement about arbitrary variables, you must not substitute concrete numeric values for those variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: giving m = 137 and n = 106 when proving for all m,n is incorrect. Treat m and n as arbitrary (chosen by the reader) and proceed using definitions and algebra; picking examples only works for existence statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: When introducing a new name for an expression, state it as a definition, not a choice
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to give a short name to an expression (e.g., t = r + s), define t directly rather than asking the reader to 'pick' it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saying 'pick any integer t where t = r + s' suggests universal instantiation. Instead write 'let t = r + s' or 'there is an integer t (namely r+s) such that ...' This clarifies that t is defined from previously existing objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: After a contradiction, state the correct universal conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: In proofs by contradiction, once you reach a contradiction, explicitly state the logical conclusion (often a universal claim) that follows from the contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable and expected to conclude with a universal claim after finishing a contradiction proof. The page notes that wording like 'thus for all nonzero real numbers x and y, ...' is appropriate after deriving a contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'contradiction sandwich'—prefer direct proof when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't wrap a direct proof in a contradiction structure whose core is already a direct proof; if the main argument gives a direct proof, present it directly instead of sandwiching it between contradiction boilerplate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the 'meat' of your contradiction proof is a valid direct proof, remove the contradiction framing and present the direct proof. This makes the argument clearer and avoids unnecessary complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use algebraic symbols but keep prose readable
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraic notation (=, +, −, superscripts, parentheses) is permitted and necessary, but ensure surrounding sentences remain grammatically correct and informative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equations to display calculations, but connect them with English sentences that explain why each calculation matters. The mugga mugga test helps ensure equations sit inside readable prose. Displayed derivations should be accompanied by explanatory sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write proofs in paragraph form, not as isolated line fragments or bullet lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should be composed as flowing paragraphs linking ideas, not as a sequence of terse equalities or step lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid proofs formatted purely as enumerated algebraic steps with no linking prose. Readers should be guided through the argument with connecting sentences that make the logical flow explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise: write less but precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer concise proofs that apply definitions directly rather than long restatements or abstract commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If students struggle, the page often recommends shortening proofs by removing unnecessary restatements of definitions and focusing on applying definitions to the chosen variables. Concision also reduces opportunities for scope errors and irrelevant statements.
